1.text: GROUPS OF DOG-BREEDING TRIBES. — The origin of dog-team driving is
1.note: Run-in heading set in small capitals per §2.13; keyed ASCII capitals, second-level heading.

2.text: still more obscure than that of the domestication of the reindeer. In Asia

3.text: there are three groups of dog-driving tribes, differing in their methods of

4.text: harnessing, the shape of harness and sledge, etc. Those belonging to the

5.text: first group, who inhabit northwestern Siberia, use a peculiar circular strap that

6.text: girds the dog’s body about the middle, like a belt, and without bands across

7.text: the shoulders, so that the dog can pull only with the hind-part of its body

8.text: (Fig. 20, a). This method of harnessing does not work well: the dogs do

9.text: not draw as heavy loads as the East Siberian teams, and they go more slowly.

10.text: East of the Lena River, and as far south as the Amur, all fishing and

11.text: seal-hunting tribes use dog-teams with uniform sledge and harness. The

12.text: sledge has three or four pairs of stanchions and a circular fore-part.¹ The
12.note: Footnote reference marker keyed as superscript ¹ U+00B9 per §2.10; machine draft had plain ASCII 1.

13.text: dogs are attached in pairs to a long, thick strap, in place of a whiffletree,

14.text: with about a fathom’s distance between the pairs; and a full team consists

15.text: of six or seven pairs. The course is directed by the voice, with special call-

16.text: words. These are understood and obeyed by the leading dog, which is trained

17.text: specially for that purpose. The harness is somewhat similar to the ordinary

18.text: horse-harness, with a breast-piece, and two or three bands across the back.

19.text: The third group of tribes — those of the Chukchee Peninsula — used,

20.text: ¹ In the collections of the Smithsonian Institution, in Washington, I saw a sledge of the Alaskan Eskimo,
20.note: Footnote opener marker keyed as superscript ¹ U+00B9 per §2.10, pairing with the reference at line 12; machine draft had plain ASCII 1. A small stray mark after "collections" at 4x looks like a comma or accent fragment but sits above the word with no corresponding letter to attach to — read as an ink artifact, not a diacritic (this is English prose).

21.text: which, curiously enough, is similar in shape to a Siberian form of sledge used by the Gilyaks of the Amur

22.text: River. Its runners are bent upwards at both ends, and are joined by a horizontal bow similar to that at the

23.text: front end of the Chukchee sledge (p. 105). The stanchions, too, are similar in shape, only their upper ends

24.text: are bent inward and fastened to cross-pieces, in the usual Eskimo manner.
